Chapter 35

Shipping it

The build, the environment, the one adapter setting that ruins your day, and what to check afterwards.

By the end of this chapter

A deployed app that survives a restart, a clock change and a Node upgrade.

Everything green locally. Four things stand between that and a URL somebody can use.

1. The gate

One command. If pnpm run verify is green, the thing is deployable; if it is not, nothing else matters. Put it in CI and make it required.

2. The adapter setting that ruins your day

Up to v5, @sveltejs/adapter-node read the trusted origin from an ORIGIN environment variable at runtime. v6, the adapter for SvelteKit 3, no longer does: the origin is baked in at build time from paths.origin in the sveltekit() options. Leave that unset and the adapter rebuilds the origin from request headers, assuming https unless PROTOCOL_HEADER says otherwise. Serve the built server over plain HTTP — node build on localhost, a container on a private network — and it computes https://… while the browser sends http://…, so every form post and remote call returns 403 "Cross-site remote requests are forbidden", from a perfectly healthy-looking app. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, setting PROTOCOL_HEADER=x-forwarded-proto and HOST_HEADER=x-forwarded-host is the other way out.

Because it is baked in at build time, PUBLIC_ORIGIN must be correct when you build, not when you start. That catches people whose CI builds an artefact and whose deploy step sets the environment.

And PUBLIC_ORIGIN is, with PUBLIC_DEFAULT_TIME_ZONE, all the build needs to know. SvelteKit validates every variable in src/env.ts when you build, because it analyses the app by running it, and the two static: true ones have to be real: "the build time value is inlined into the bundle". The three private, dynamic ones — DATABASE_URL, ORIGIN and BETTER_AUTH_SECRET — are read from the environment when the server starts, and chapter 15 used the docs' own opt-out, building from $app/env, so that they may be missing while building and are required the moment the server boots.

The two modules that read them honour the same flag. The database module opens an in-memory database while building and skips its pragmas, and auth.ts hands Better Auth a throwaway secret; neither reaches anything real. So the build command names what the build uses, and nothing else:

We ran exactly that, in a copy of the project with no .env and none of the private variables set: the build finished, and no database file appeared. Better Auth prints one warning on the way, that its base URL is not set, which is true while building and stops being true when the server starts with ORIGIN. Starting the result the same way, without the private variables, stops at once with SvelteKit's env_invalid naming all three — the check has moved to where it belongs, not gone.

Why not hand the build placeholders

That was this chapter's first answer, and it is still the one you will find in a great many projects. Without the opt-out, a build given only the public variables stopped at Analysing routes with env_invalid, so the recipe fed it DATABASE_URL=:memory:, a dummy ORIGIN and a made-up secret. Each placeholder had a trap. DATABASE_URL=placeholder got past validation and then failed the build with LibsqlError: URL_INVALID from a generated chunk, because the database module handed it to createClient the moment it loaded. And a URL libSQL could parse was used, not merely checked: a file: URL created the file, and a remote one was sent the WAL pragma, so a build run with production's environment loaded talked to production. Placeholders made the build need to know about variables it has no use for. building makes it not need them.

3. Dependencies versus devDependencies

adapter-node bundles devDependencies into the server build, with Rolldown since v6, and leaves dependencies to be installed beside it. @libsql/client loads a native binary at runtime and cannot be bundled.

Both are needed. Get it wrong and the app builds, deploys, starts, and dies on the first request with Cannot find module '@libsql/linux-x64-gnu'.

4. Pin the runtime

This app depends on the runtime's time zone database and on Intl, so "whatever Node the host feels like" is a real risk. Pinning also makes the ICU-version problem from chapter 32 a decision you make rather than one that happens to you.

Migrations on deploy

Migrations run before the server starts, and they run from the checked-in SQL — never from drizzle-kit push, which compares your schema file to the live database and decides what to do about the difference. That is a fine command for your laptop and a terrible one to point at production.

What to check once it is up

  1. View source on the booking page. The studio name and services should be in the HTML. If you see "Loading…", a pending snippet has escaped onto a page-level boundary.
  2. Book something. Then book the same slot from a second browser and confirm the refusal is polite.
  3. Check the diary updates live in a window you have left open.
  4. Set your phone to another time zone and load the booking page. The times should move; the studio's zone should be named.
  5. Restart the process. Everything should still be there — and PRAGMA journal_mode should still say wal.

What you built

A booking platform that tells the truth about time, cannot double-book, updates itself, works without JavaScript, and is tested well enough that you would deploy it on a Friday.

The three ideas worth carrying to the next thing you build, none of which are about SvelteKit:

  1. Know which layer is the guarantee. Halfpast has three defences against double-booking and exactly one of them is load-bearing. Being able to say which is the difference between a system you trust and one you hope about.
  2. Make the invisible testable. now is an argument, the availability engine is pure, and both daylight-saving transitions run in a fifth of a second. Nothing else about this project would have been provable otherwise.
  3. A client-side check is a courtesy; a server-side check is a control. Build both, and write the test that removes the courtesy.

Checkpoint

pnpm run verify is green, the app is deployed, and all five post-deploy checks pass.
